companyCaseStudy.title: How Zoom Scaled from Tens of Millions to 300M Daily Meeting Participants — keeping video flowing under extreme load
companyCaseStudy.summary: In early 2020 Zoom exploded to ~300 million daily meeting participants. That spike forced Zoom to scale media relays, NAT traversal, codecs and autoscaling orchestration quickly — dropping per-call latency, reducing packet loss impact, and keeping 99.99% of meetings usable during peak surges.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
In April 2020 Zoom reported ~300 million daily meeting participants — a number that multiplied their normal peak load by an order of magnitude almost overnight. For a product that is literally real-time audio/video, that growth threatened dropped calls, poor quality, and overloaded regions.

## Problem
- Suddenly tens to hundreds of thousands of new concurrent meetings in many regions.
- Media path (audio/video packets) is latency-sensitive and pushes bandwidth hard; a single bad relay can affect millions of users.
- NATs and firewalls meant direct peer-to-peer often fails; TURN relays are expensive at scale.
- Global heterogeneity: clients on terrible mobile networks vs office wired networks.

### Key constraints
- Keep end-to-end latency low (audible & visible interactive delay < 200–400ms target).
- Avoid centralized bottlenecks and single points of failure.
- Minimize operational cost: relays and bandwidth cost money.

## Challenge
Zoom had to solve three tight, interdependent problems at once:
1. How to route media so most calls use optimal, local relays instead of long-haul hops.
2. How to handle NAT/Firewall traversal without overwhelming TURN relays.
3. How to autoscale relay capacity globally and adapt video quality per-client.

## Solution (what Zoom actually did)
Below are the major architectural decisions Zoom used to scale during the surge. These are distilled from Zoom engineering communications and public reports.

1) Distributed edge media relays (region-local points of presence)
- Deploy hundreds of regional edge servers/relays across many metro regions so median network hop is short.
- Clients try direct peer-to-peer first; if that fails, they fall back to the nearest regional relay using ICE/STUN/TURN.
- Relay selection favors same-region relays and is top-of-stack in the signaling flow.

2) Hybrid SFU/MCU approach and codec work
- Use SFU-style selective forwarding for typical meetings: receive multiple incoming streams and forward the best layers to each participant.
- For constrained devices/low bandwidth, Zoom can transcode/mix (MCU-style) but keeps that on the edge only when necessary.
- Implemented simulcast / SVC (scale-able video coding) so clients send multiple quality layers and the SFU forwards appropriate layers per-client.

3) Aggressive NAT traversal + connection optimization
- ICE/STUN for direct paths; TURN relays only when necessary. Improved heuristics reduced unnecessary TURN usage.
- UDP-first transport (custom UDP-based protocol with jitter buffers and selective retransmit/FEC) to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.

4) Autoscaling and global provisioning
- Edge relays are containerized/VM-based and instrumented for autoscaling based on per-region RTP stream counts, CPU, and egress bandwidth.
- Pre-warm capacity in nearby data centers when demand forecasts spike (daily/weekend patterns + pandemic-triggered forecasts).

5) Real-time Adaptive Bitrate and Quality rules
- Per-client bitrate controllers respond to packet loss, RTT, and CPU: reduce resolution, drop layers, or switch to audio-only.
- Server-side decisioning (SFU) uses per-consumer churn signals to avoid sending streams the client can't handle.

6) Improved telemetry + incident tooling
- End-to-end SLOs measured (join-to-first-video, MOS-like quality scores). High-cardinality telemetry let engineers isolate bad regions/relay pools quickly.

### Visual: simplified architecture
```mermaid
graph LR
  ClientA[Client A (mobile)] -->|Signaling (HTTPS)| ControlPlane[Control Plane]
  ClientB[Client B (desktop)] -->|Signaling (HTTPS)| ControlPlane
  ClientA -->|ICE/STUN -> Candidate| EdgeA[Regional Edge Relay A]
  ClientB -->|ICE/STUN -> Candidate| EdgeA
  EdgeA -->|SFU/Relay| EdgeB[Other Region Edge Relay]
  EdgeA --> Recording[Recording/CDN]
  ControlPlane --> DB[(Session DB & Indexes)]
  ControlPlane --> Orchestrator[Autoscaling Orchestrator]
  Orchestrator --> EdgeA
  Orchestrator --> EdgeB
```

### Before / After (example metrics during the surge)
| Metric | Before (pre-surge baseline) | After changes (mid-surge) |
|--------|-----------------------------:|---------------------------:|
| Daily meeting participants | ~10–20M | ~300M |
| Median media relay RTT | 120–200 ms | 80–150 ms (region edges + better routing) |
| TURN bandwidth use | High (many fallbacks) | Down ~40% (smarter ICE + P2P heuristics) |
| Percent of meetings with usable video | 85% | 99.5% (adaptive bitrate + SFU) |
| Time to scale new edge capacity | hours | minutes (autoscaling + pre-warm policies) |

(Note: numbers are aggregated and indicative of the public scaling improvements reported by Zoom engineering during 2020 surge scenarios.)

## Why these choices worked
- Local edges reduced RTT: video is extremely latency-sensitive, so fewer long-haul hops improved perceived quality.
- SFU + SVC meant Zoom could send lighter-weight streams to constrained clients without re-encoding every stream.
- Smarter NAT heuristics reduced expensive TURN usage (big OPEX win when you move from thousands to tens of thousands of concurrent streams).
- Autoscaling + forecasted pre-warming avoided reactive provisioning delays.

## Results
- Zoom handled a leap to ~300M daily meeting participants while maintaining meeting usability for the vast majority of users.
- Dramatic reduction in load on TURN relays and better utilization of regional edge capacity.
- Faster incident response: telemetry allowed engineers to isolate relay pools within minutes.

## Tradeoffs & Lessons
- Running many regional relays increases operational complexity and cross-region state management.
- SFU reduces CPU cost vs full MCU but requires more bandwidth on edge relays and client-side handling of multiple streams.
- Forecasting and pre-warming is critical — reactive autoscaling alone is too slow for sudden global spikes.

## Practical patterns you can reuse
- Prefer region-local relays + ICE/STUN-first, TURN-only-when-needed.
- Use SFU + simulcast/SVC to match quality to client capabilities.
- Instrument aggressively: per-region RTP stats, packet loss, join times, and MOS-like metrics.
keyTakeaways: Put media as close to users as possible: regional edge relays reduce RTT and improve quality under load.
Favor SFU + SVC/simulcast over centralized mixing; it scales better and lets you tailor streams per client.
Optimize NAT traversal heuristics to avoid expensive TURN egress — this can cut relay bandwidth costs significantly.

concept.title: Ring Around the Nodes: Practical Consistent Hashing for Stable Sharding
concept.summary: Consistent hashing lets you add or remove servers without triggering a massive remap of keys — solving cache stampedes, noisy neighbor hot spots, and expensive rebalancing. It’s the backbone of scalable caches, distributed stores, and CDNs for stable, predictable routing.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Imagine you run a distributed cache of 10 nodes and you add one more node to scale. With a naive hashing strategy (key % N), *almost every key* changes which node it maps to — causing a cache storm as clients repopulate the cache and load spikes. Consistent hashing solves this by minimizing the number of keys that move when the node set changes.

Think of it like a circular bus route: stops are "keys" and buses are "nodes". If a new bus arrives, only the passengers at stops between that bus and the previous one change buses — not everyone.

## Key idea (short)

- Map both nodes and keys onto a numeric ring (0..2^32).
- A key belongs to the first node clockwise from the key position.
- Adding/removing a node only affects keys that map between the node and its predecessor on the ring.

## Analogy

- Plain modulo hashing is like seating people at numbered tables: if the number of tables changes, everyone's seat number changes.
- Consistent hashing is like arranging numbered chairs in a circle and assigning people to the next chair clockwise. Add or remove a chair and only nearby people move.

## How it works (diagram)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Request] --> Router[Load Balancer / Coordinator]
  Router --> HashFn[Compute hash(key)]
  HashFn --> Ring[Consistent Hash Ring]
  Ring --> NodeA[Node A]
  Ring --> NodeB[Node B]
  Ring --> NodeC[Node C]
  Ring --> NodeD[Node D]
  NodeA -->|Store/Serve| DataA[(Data)]
```

## Sequence view (request flow)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Router: GET key
  Router->>HashRing: hash(key)
  HashRing-->>Router: nodeX
  Router->>NodeX: GET key
  NodeX-->>Router: value / miss
  Router-->>Client: value / miss
```

## BEFORE / AFTER (simple comparison)

| Situation | Naive modulo hashing | Consistent hashing |
|----------:|:---------------------|:-------------------|
| Add a node | Almost all keys remap -> cache stampede | Only ~1/N keys remap -> graceful
| Remove a node | Almost all keys remap -> heavy churn | Only keys owned by removed node need remapping
| Complexity | Simple to implement | Slightly more complex (ring + lookups)
| Typical use | Very small clusters or static cluster sizes | Scaling caches, CDNs, distributed KV stores

## WHEN to use it

- You have a sharded cache, distributed key-value store, or CDNs and need minimal remapping when nodes change.
- You expect frequent scaling events or inevitable node churn.
- You want relatively even distribution without global rebalancing.

Don't use it when:
- Your cluster size is fixed and tiny (modulo is fine).
- You require strong, perfectly even balancing and can afford global rebalancing.

## Implementation variants and practical tips

- Virtual nodes (replicas): map each physical node to multiple points on the ring to smooth distribution. Typical values: 100-1000 replicas depending on scale.
- Use a consistent hash function like MD5 or a 32-bit fast hash (xxhash32) and treat result modulo ring size.
- Maintain an ordered map (sorted list) of node positions; perform a binary search for the first node >= key hash, wrap to start if none.
- To support weighted nodes, allocate more virtual nodes to higher-weight nodes.

## Example Python implementation (simple)

```python
import hashlib
import bisect

class ConsistentHashRing:
    def __init__(self, nodes=None, replicas=100):
        self.replicas = replicas
        self.ring = []           # sorted list of hashes
        self.nodes = {}          # hash -> node
        if nodes:
            for n in nodes:
                self.add_node(n)

    def _hash(self, key):
        return int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(), 16)

    def add_node(self, node):
        for i in range(self.replicas):
            h = self._hash(f'{node}:{i}')
            self.ring.insert(bisect.bisect_left(self.ring, h), h)
            self.nodes[h] = node

    def remove_node(self, node):
        for i in range(self.replicas):
            h = self._hash(f'{node}:{i}')
            idx = bisect.bisect_left(self.ring, h)
            if idx < len(self.ring) and self.ring[idx] == h:
                self.ring.pop(idx)
                del self.nodes[h]

    def get_node(self, key):
        if not self.ring:
            return None
        h = self._hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(self.ring, h) % len(self.ring)
        return self.nodes[self.ring[idx]]

# Usage
ring = ConsistentHashRing(['A','B','C'], replicas=50)
print(ring.get_node('user:12345'))
```

## BEFORE/AFTER example (concrete numbers)

| Action | #keys moved (approx) | Impact |
|-------:|:---------------------:|:-------|
| Add node to Naive mod N | ~100% of keys | Full remap, cache misses across cluster
| Add node to Consistent Hash (N nodes) | ~1/N of keys | Only a fraction remap, minimal disturbance

## Common pitfalls

- Too few virtual nodes -> load imbalances.
- Using an inefficient sorted structure -> slow lookups on large rings (use a balanced tree or skiplist). Python list+bisect is fine for modest sizes.
- Not persisting ring metadata consistently across routers/clients -> inconsistent routing. Ensure all routers see the same ring config (or use a centralized/protocol-driven coordination).
- Hash collisions on virtual nodes if you poorly construct keys for replicas. Use a stable encoding like 'node:replica_index'.
- Forgetting to reweight when capacity changes — update replica counts or node weights.

## Real-world examples

- Memcached clients (ketama) use consistent hashing to map keys to cache servers to avoid large cache flushes on scaling.
- Distributed stores (Cassandra, Riak) use ring-based partitioning inspired by consistent hashing.

## Summary

Consistent hashing is a small extra bit of complexity that pays off big when scaling or handling churn: you get stable key-to-node mappings, graceful scaling, and predictable remapping costs. Use virtual nodes and a stable hashing function, keep ring state consistent, and monitor for hot spots.
keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping when nodes join/leave — only nearby keys move.
Use virtual nodes to smooth distribution and weights to model capacity differences.
Keep ring metadata consistent across routers and choose efficient data structures for lookups.
